title: Priority-fair adaptive windowing and queue for real-time console events
creator: Diego Ramos
description: Problem: Console telemetry spikes (customer dashboards, per-token billing, and rollout traces) are causing tail latency regressions during bursts and noisy tenants. Current ingestion treats events FIFO with simple bulk-sharding, which leads to head-of-line blocking when a tenant or route emits large bursts of low-priority data. Goal: introduce a priority-fair, adaptive-windowing queue and light-weight local aggregation layer before the global stream to reduce p95/p99 ingestion latency while preserving per-tenant fairness and cost accounting. Targets: p95 end-to-end ingest < 200ms for interactive routes during typical burst patterns, bounded upstream queue growth, and no loss of observability (trace IDs preserved).
acceptance_criteria: New ingress queue implements 3 configurable priority bands (high/normal/low) with token-bucket shaping per-tenant and per-route.
Adaptive windowing reduces per-tenant batching delay to meet p95 latency SLO under 90th percentile burst sizes from log analysis.
Hot-tenant mitigation limits downstream concurrency but preserves fair share across tenants (no tenant can starve others for >1s).
End-to-end telemetry preserved: trace/span and customer IDs flow through queue unchanged and appear in Console dashboards.
Load tests show 30-45% reduction in p99 ingest latency on synthetic burst scenarios compared to baseline, and cost of CPU overhead < 8% on proxy nodes.
implementation_notes: Architecture: place a lightweight local queue + priority scheduler at the front of each ingestion proxy; use NATS JetStream as durable backing for cross-zone failover to minimize tail amplification.
Per-tenant shaping: Redis-based token buckets keyed by tenant->route with leaky replenishment; fall back to local in-memory counters when Redis unavailable to avoid blocking requests.
Adaptive windowing: dynamically adjust flush interval per-priority band using moving-average of incoming rate and observed latency; cap window to 50ms for high priority and 250ms for low.
Graceful degradation: if downstream backpressure exceeds threshold, switch low-priority traffic to sampled-aggregate mode (emit counters instead of full events) and surface outage via console alert.
Compatibility: maintain existing Kafka consumer groups for downstream pipelines; the new local queue will batch into existing Avro envelopes to avoid downstream parsing changes.
test_plan: Unit tests for scheduler fairness and token-bucket edge cases.
Chaos tests: Redis unavailability and JetStream latency spikes to validate fallback mode.
Performance tests: compare p95/p99 ingest latency under recorded burst traces from 2026-01-09 incident and synthetic traffic with 10k concurrent sources.
Canary rollout: start with 5% traffic in us-east-1 then expand to 25%/50%/100% with automated rollback on >2x p95 degradation.
notes: 2026-02-05: Kickoff meeting — aligned on NATS JetStream as durable layer to reduce write amplification vs Kafka for short-lived windowed batches.
2026-02-12: Spike implemented: local scheduler prototype reduced p95 by 22% on desktop telemetry trace. See spike notes: https://docs.redwood/internal/spikes/priority-queue-2026-02-12
2026-02-25: Design review feedback (PM): expose tenant-level QoS knobs in Console; Design: add UI toggle for sampled-aggregate mode.
2026-03-02: Engineering review: trade-off between Redis-backed accuracy vs in-memory fast path. Decided on hybrid approach with conservative fallback to sampling when Redis latency >50ms.

2026-03-08: Load test run 2026-03-07-18: saw 40% p99 reduction for normal priority and only 6% CPU overhead on ingest-proxy fleet. Test artifacts: https://perf.redwood.internal/console/priority-queue/2026-03-07

2026-03-10: Blocker identified — JetStream client library had a reconnect regression at 10k streams; temporary workaround: reduce stream count via tenant coalescing; ENG-201419 created to track client upgrade work.
